author: high
claim: In the Boolean lattice of subsets of [n], every maximal chain can be encoded by a permutation of [n], and a fixed set A of size k belongs to exactly k!(n-k)! maximal chains.
evidence: Given an ordering (x_1,...,x_n) of [n], the initial segments empty set, {x_1},...,{x_1,...,x_n} form a maximal chain, and every maximal chain gives a unique ordering by recording the element added at each step. Such a chain contains a fixed k-set A exactly when the first k ordered elements are precisely the elements of A. There are k! orders of those elements and (n-k)! orders of the remaining elements, hence k!(n-k)! chains.

author: high
claim: If a family of subsets is an antichain, then each maximal chain contains at most one member of the family; double-counting incidences with maximal chains yields the LYM inequality sum over A in the family of 1/binom(n,|A|) at most 1.
evidence: Any two distinct members of one chain are comparable by inclusion, so an antichain contributes at most one incidence to each of the n! maximal chains. A member A of size k contributes k!(n-k)! incidences. Thus the total incidence count is sum_A |A|!(n-|A|)! and is at most n!. Divide by n! and use |A|!(n-|A|)!/n!=1/binom(n,|A|).

glossary.A: a member of the antichain family

author: high
claim: For every integer k with 0 at most k at most n, binom(n,k) is at most binom(n,floor(n/2)).
evidence: For 0<=k<n, binom(n,k+1)/binom(n,k)=(n-k)/(k+1). This ratio is at least 1 exactly when k<=(n-1)/2 and at most 1 exactly when k>=(n-1)/2. Hence the binomial coefficients increase up to a middle index and then decrease. By symmetry binom(n,k)=binom(n,n-k), the value at floor(n/2) is a maximum (equal also to the ceiling middle value when n is odd).
